name: Gareth Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. Your answers are confidential. What does your day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and became a manager at a large vehicle-rental company this year. Four dispatchers report to me; we set collection times, arrange replacement vans and settle the arguments when a customer arrives before a vehicle is ready. I have a bachelor’s degree, but I still miss things in the weekly capacity report and ask the old team lead to check it. I use AI tools every day to compare bookings and draft notices, then phone the depot before I promise a van.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife is a pharmacist, and our children are eight and thirteen. We have a mortgage and about eleven months of expenses saved; my pay is high for this manager job because I cover weekends. There are plenty of transport and service management posts nearby. I like a useful machine, but I want it judged by whether a customer gets the keys on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell dispatch that AI Plateau is a tidier booking screen. We still need a depot worker to confirm the van is clean and has its keys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my pay and post stay secure. My wife and I have saved enough to handle a slow month, and I cannot see a small tool replacing a manager who sorts a failed handover. I would still watch the mortgage, as anyone should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I’d keep the morning depot call and use my existing AI comparison to flag double bookings. If a minor feature arrives, I’d test it against ten old handovers before changing the live queue. We would keep the monthly mortgage-overpayment we already make from full-pay months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. A screen improvement might make Saturdays easier, and our bills have room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the screen miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Saturday was a mess. A van showed available, but its keys were still with the cleaning team. The customer was standing at the counter with children and luggage. I arranged a different van, then fixed the booking record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the firm owns this system. I will try the approved feature at work and report what breaks. Our household money is for the mortgage and children, not a company experiment.

say: **AI Plateau** tidies bookings but does not confirm keys and clean vans.
I would keep the **depot call** before making a promise.
think: My **post and pay** look secure under a small tool change.
Our **savings** can cover a slow month while the mortgage continues.
do: **Keep** the morning depot call and double-booking check.
**Test** a minor feature against ten old handovers before live use.
**Continue** monthly mortgage overpayments in full-pay months.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and bills in this picture.
S0.quote: A van showed available, but its keys were still with the cleaning team.
fieldNote: His **eleven-month reserve**, two wages and many local openings support calm under a minor change.
Daily AI use remains tied to **physical handovers** and the keys a depot worker confirms.

steps.text: Keep calling the depot before promising a replacement van
Test the booking feature against ten old vehicle handovers
Continue mortgage overpayments in months with full pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can book vehicles, plan routes, write notices and answer easy customer questions. I want the company to measure failed handovers before it declares a smaller dispatch team a success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, those screen tasks are most of my new manager day. I am quick with tools but still learning to manage capacity, so a smaller dispatch desk could remove my post. We have savings and nearby jobs, yet I would miss the weekend pay that supports our mortgage overpayments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d run a four-week trial of the company’s new booking model and count customers who arrive without a ready vehicle. I’d take its paid training if the director approves my place. If dispatch posts shrink after rollout, I’d apply for a posted depot-operations supervisor role only if the salary and weekend rota work for my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my post, but I can test a tool and check real openings. I would rather show a failed handover than argue about whether AI is good or bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which failure would you record first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van with the missing keys. The dashboard called it available, while the customer waited nearly an hour. I would track actual collection time, not just a completed booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why depot operations?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It includes checking vehicles and coaching people at the counter, work I have done before. The rota may be harder on my wife’s pharmacy hours, though. I would read a real offer before moving.

say: **Booking automation** should be measured against failed handovers and the time customers really wait.
A completed reservation is not a **ready vehicle** when the keys are still missing.
think: My new manager post could go if the **dispatch desk shrinks**.
Savings and local jobs help, but **weekend pay** matters to our mortgage plan.
do: **Run** a four-week booking trial and count unready vehicles.
**Take** paid model training if my place is approved.
**Apply** for depot supervision only if salary and family rota work.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible post cut, with options to test.
S1.quote: I would track actual collection time, not just a completed booking.
fieldNote: He welcomes a **measured trial**, but knows tool skill alone may not protect a junior manager role.
The **depot fallback** needs a real salary and rota that fit his wife’s hours.

steps.text: Run four-week booking trial and count unready vans at collection
Take paid booking-model training if director approves his place
Apply for depot supervisor vacancy only if salary and family rota work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 could handle almost any booking and capacity report. I would ask for a clear cut date and a list of depot jobs with their wages, rather than tell people all dispatch seats are safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full thinking AI in 2028 could do my screen work before capable robots handle vehicles around 2031. I expect the dispatch desk to contract, and my recently won manager post might go. With eleven months saved, my wife’s salary and local openings, I can search without missing the mortgage immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I’d ask the director for a written staffing plan and compare three advertised depot manager posts with my current weekend pay. I’d apply only to posts that include real vehicle checks and a rota my wife and I can cover. If AGI arrives in 2028 and I am cut, I’d accept a confirmed depot offer if the pay covers our mortgage and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing the role I worked for. I am not helpless, but I will not promise my dispatchers a place that has not been posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could a depot job also change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Depot reports and schedules would face AGI in 2028; robots around 2031 could then change physical vehicle checks. I am looking for a current job offer, not a forever-safe trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say I may work at a depot instead of the office, but they will stay at their school for now. My wife and I would not change pickup until we had an actual rota. We can pay the mortgage while I look.

say: **AGI by 2028** requires cut dates and posted depot wages.
I would not promise **safe dispatch seats** without evidence.
think: My screen role faces AGI in **2028**, before vehicle robots around 2031.
My post might go, but **savings and local jobs** allow a search.
do: **Request** a written staff plan next month.
**Apply** for depot posts only with real vehicle checks and a family-compatible rota.
**Accept** a confirmed depot offer after 2028 only if pay covers mortgage and childcare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing a new role, with time to search.
S2.quote: Depot reports and schedules would face AGI in 2028; robots around 2031 could then change physical vehicle checks.
fieldNote: He sees **depot paperwork** exposed in 2028 and physical checks vulnerable after robots arrive around 2031.
His **strong cushion** supports an offer search but does not make a vacancy certain.

steps.text: Apply for depot posts only with real vehicle checks and family-compatible rota
Accept confirmed depot offer after 2028 only if pay covers mortgage and childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives time to test who still fixes a failed handover when the booking system has already said yes. I’d want depot staff involved in any new capacity rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My booking and report work could go in 2031, and a depot manager’s paperwork is exposed then too. Robots able to inspect and move vehicles arrive around 2034, so the hands-on part changes later. I have local options, though the best paying depot posts may be filled when I need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From January 2027 I’d take a paid six-week depot assignment if the company offers my current salary and covers my dispatch desk. I’d use the trial to learn vehicle readiness checks from depot staff rather than buy a generic course. After 2031 I’d apply for a depot operations vacancy only if its pay, weekend rota and childcare costs work for my wife and me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the desk could still go. Five years lets me test the physical work before I sign up for another management title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn in six weeks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How the cleaning and servicing teams mark a van ready, and where the keys actually go. I still miss details in the capacity report. I would ask a depot worker to correct my checklist each week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company will not cover your desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep supervising dispatch and ask for two paid depot days instead. I will not leave four people without someone to settle customer complaints. The trial only works if both teams have cover.

say: **Five years** allows a paid depot trial with staff input.
I’d test **vehicle readiness** before trusting new capacity rules.
think: Dispatch and depot paperwork face **2031 AGI**, before vehicle robots around 2034.
Local posts exist, but a **well-paid vacancy** is uncertain.
do: **Take** a paid six-week depot assignment if salary and dispatch cover hold.
**Learn** vehicle readiness checks from depot staff during the approved trial.
**Apply** after 2031 only if depot pay, rota and childcare costs work.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the desk, with time to test depot work.
S3.quote: I still miss details in the capacity report.
fieldNote: He admits a **current skill gap** despite daily AI use and high pay.
The depot trial needs **salary protection** and desk cover, with childcare and rota limits on later posts.

steps.text: Take six-week depot assignment only with current salary and dispatch cover
Learn van readiness checks from depot staff during the paid trial
Apply after 2031 for depot post only if pay rota and childcare costs work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives companies a decade to publish real jobs and let people try them while still paid. I would judge a training plan by whether a driver actually gets a ready van, not by a slide showing hours saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our pay continues, my wife and I could pay the mortgage down and keep more than eleven months set aside. My dispatch reports and depot paperwork still face thinking AI in 2036; vehicle robots come around 2039. I do not need to leave a well-paid job now, but I will watch which roles still include real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the depot call and continue the full-pay-month mortgage overpayment. Each spring I’d review posted transport operations jobs and ask a depot worker what the role actually does. Before 2036 I’d take a paid site rotation only if it keeps my salary and family rota; after AGI arrives I’d stay only while the work and pay remain real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years. We have time, savings and other employers to consider.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put savings into a vehicle business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not from one good year of dispatch pay. I would look at repair costs, insurance and how many rentals a small operator really wins. My father started a shop with careful books; I learned that part, not a taste for guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the rota changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife and I would draw out the school week again and check who collects the eight-year-old. We would not accept a shift pattern that leaves a child waiting. By 2036 the children will be about eighteen and twenty-three, so that specific pickup will have passed.

say: A **decade** should bring paid trials and real posted roles.
I would judge new tools by **ready vans**, not slides.
think: Both wages could reduce the **mortgage** and preserve a strong reserve.
Dispatch and depot paperwork face **2036 AGI**, before vehicle robots around 2039.
do: **Keep** depot calls and full-pay mortgage overpayments in 2026.
**Review** posted transport roles each spring with depot staff input.
**Take** a paid site rotation with protected salary and family rota; stay after 2036 only while work and pay remain real.
feel: I feel **calm** about the next few years with time and savings.
S4.quote: My father started a shop with careful books; I learned that part, not a taste for guessing.
fieldNote: His **traditional outlook** favours a tested business calculation and work over speculative investment.
He updates the **children’s ages** by 2036 instead of treating pickup as a permanent condition.

steps.text: Keep calling depots before promising vehicles through 2026
Continue mortgage overpayments only in full-pay months
Review posted transport operations roles each spring
Take paid depot rotation only with salary and family rota protected

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our dispatch desk could shrink before I have enough depot experience. A written cut date, a paid depot trial and posted wages for real openings would help. Eleven months saved lets us choose, not pretend every job is safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the driver whether the van has keys when the system says ready. A booking is only complete when a customer can drive away. The handover is where the promise is tested.

headlineQuote: A booking is only complete when a customer can drive away.
portrait: **Gareth, 43**, is a newly promoted dispatch manager at a large vehicle-rental company with a bachelor’s degree.
His **high pay**, pharmacist wife, eleven-month reserve and many local jobs support a mortgage and two school-age children.
He uses **AI daily** but admits he still misses capacity-report details and checks readiness with depot staff.
He is **calm** under AI Plateau, anxious about 2028 desk cuts and tests a paid depot assignment conditionally.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink his new dispatch post before he has enough depot experience.
whatWouldHelp: A written **cut date**, paid depot trial and posted wages for real openings would help.
